seeds.title: Pythagorean triple: a^2+b^2=c^2 -- the Pythagorean theorem for integer sides
seeds.statement: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three positive integers (a, b, c) satisfying a^2 + b^2 = c^2 -- the integer instance of the Pythagorean theorem, that in a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. Euclid proved the theorem in general (for any right triangle, not just integer sides) in Elements, Book I, Proposition 47, using the 'windmill' figure; Proposition 48 gives the converse. The smallest examples are (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (20,21,29). This is a checkable arithmetic definition, not folklore, and the checker VERIFIES a^2+b^2=c^2 by direct computation for the specific triple given.
seeds.canonical_statement: (a,b,c) is a Pythagorean triple iff a^2 + b^2 = c^2, all positive integers
seeds.source_citation: Euclid (fl. 300 BCE), Elements, Book I, Proposition 47 (the Pythagorean theorem, proved via the 'windmill' figure) and Proposition 48 (its converse). D.E. Joyce, 'Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 47', Clark University (mathcs.clarku.edu); Weisstein, 'Pythagorean Triple', Wolfram MathWorld; Wikipedia 'Pythagorean triple'.
seeds.author: Euclid

verification.method: Computationally verified: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (20,21,29), (7,24,25), (9,40,41), (12,35,37), (6,8,10), (9,12,15) all satisfy a^2+b^2=c^2 exactly (0 counterexamples). Elements Book I Prop. 47/48 attribution confirmed against D.E. Joyce's Clark University transcription and Britannica 'Euclid's Windmill' (web-checked 2026-07-06).

seeds.title: Primitive Pythagorean triple: gcd(a,b,c)=1 -- the 'reduced' triples every other triple scales from
seeds.statement: A Pythagorean triple (a,b,c) is PRIMITIVE when gcd(a,b,c) = 1 -- no integer greater than 1 divides all three. Every Pythagorean triple is an integer multiple k of exactly one primitive triple: e.g. (6,8,10) = 2*(3,4,5) and (9,12,15) = 3*(3,4,5) are both non-primitive multiples of the primitive (3,4,5). The smallest primitive triples are (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25), (20,21,29). This is a checkable arithmetic definition, and the checker VERIFIES both a^2+b^2=c^2 AND gcd(a,b,c)=1 by direct computation for the specific triple given.
seeds.source_citation: Weisstein, 'Primitive Pythagorean Triple', Wolfram MathWorld (mathworld.wolfram.com/PrimitivePythagoreanTriple.html) -- definition gcd(a,b,c)=1, and every non-primitive triple is an integer multiple of a unique primitive one. Wikipedia 'Pythagorean triple', section 'Elementary properties of primitive Pythagorean triples'.
seeds.author: classical / MathWorld

verification.method: Computationally verified: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (20,21,29), (7,24,25), (9,40,41), (12,35,37) all have gcd(a,b,c)=1 (primitive); (6,8,10) has gcd=2 and (9,12,15) has gcd=3 (both non-primitive multiples of (3,4,5)). Definition confirmed against Wolfram MathWorld 'Primitive Pythagorean Triple' (web-checked 2026-07-06).

seeds.title: Euclid's formula: (m^2-n^2, 2mn, m^2+n^2) generates every primitive Pythagorean triple
seeds.statement: For integers m > n > 0, the triple (a,b,c) = (m^2-n^2, 2mn, m^2+n^2) always satisfies a^2+b^2=c^2 (an algebraic identity), and is PRIMITIVE exactly when m and n are coprime and of opposite parity (one even, one odd). Conversely, every primitive Pythagorean triple arises this way for a unique such pair (m,n). The construction is recorded in Euclid's Elements, Book X, Lemma 1 (immediately preceding Proposition 29), where Euclid uses it to build the numbers needed for that proposition. Examples: (m,n)=(2,1) gives (3,4,5); (3,2) gives (5,12,13); (4,3) gives (7,24,25); (6,5) gives (11,60,61). The checker COMPUTES the construction for the given m,n and VERIFIES both the identity and (when the preconditions hold) primitivity by direct computation.
seeds.canonical_statement: m>n>0, gcd(m,n)=1, m-n odd => (m^2-n^2, 2mn, m^2+n^2) is a primitive Pythagorean triple
seeds.source_citation: Euclid (fl. 300 BCE), Elements, Book X, Lemma 1 (preceding Proposition 29) -- the construction of what is now called 'Euclid's formula' for Pythagorean triples. D.E. Joyce, 'Euclid's Elements, Book X, Proposition 29', Clark University (mathcs.clarku.edu); Wikipedia 'Pythagorean triple', section 'Euclid's formula' (states the Book X, Lemma 1 provenance and the coprime/opposite-parity primitivity condition); Weisstein, 'Primitive Pythagorean Triple', Wolfram MathWorld.
seeds.author: Euclid

verification.method: Computationally verified: (m,n) = (2,1),(3,2),(4,1),(5,2),(4,3),(5,4),(6,1),(6,5) all satisfy m>n>0, coprime, opposite parity, and every resulting (a,b,c) satisfies a^2+b^2=c^2 with gcd(a,b,c)=1 (primitive) -- 0 counterexamples. (m,n)=(4,2) (both even, not coprime) was checked to correctly yield a NON-primitive result (7,24,25 scaled... actually (12,16,20)=4x(3,4,5)), confirming the preconditions are load-bearing. Book X Lemma 1 provenance confirmed against D.E. Joyce's Clark University transcription and Wikipedia 'Pythagorean triple' (web-checked 2026-07-06).

seeds.title: The 3-4-5 triangle as Osiris-Isis-Horus -- Plutarch's mystical reading (speculative LEAP)
seeds.statement: That (3,4,5) satisfies 3^2+4^2=5^2 and is a primitive Pythagorean triple is a real, checkable arithmetic fact. The further claim that this triangle carries cosmic or mystical significance is a numerological/theological interpretation, not mathematics. Plutarch (c. 46-120 CE), in De Iside et Osiride (Moralia), section 56, describes the Egyptians holding a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 in special honor, likening the upright (3) to the male principle Osiris, the base (4) to the female principle Isis, and the hypotenuse (5) to their child Horus -- 'the perfected result' -- and adds numerological commentary (three as the first perfect odd number, four as a square, five as compounded of three and two). This reading has no mathematical content beyond the arithmetic identity itself and NO promotion path to 'established'. M8 verifies the arithmetic and must label any 'sacred' significance as a separate, non-mathematical claim it never proved.
seeds.source_citation: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (Moralia), section 56 -- the Osiris/Isis/Horus reading of the 3-4-5 triangle, cited here as the SOURCE of the significance claim, not as mathematical evidence. Perseus Digital Library, Plutarch De Iside et Osiride section 56 (perseus.tufts.edu). The arithmetic fact itself is the established one (see pythagorean-triple-definition, primitive-pythagorean-triple-definition); the 'sacred' reading is not established and has no promotion path.

seeds.title: Pythagorean triples were known over a millennium before Pythagoras -- Plimpton 322
seeds.statement: Despite the name, Pythagorean triples were known and systematically tabulated long before Pythagoras (fl. 6th century BCE) was born. Plimpton 322 is an Old Babylonian clay tablet (c. 1900-1600 BCE, held at Columbia University) containing a table of 15 rows of numbers in cuneiform sexagesimal notation that scholars agree encodes Pythagorean triples (or the closely related ratios needed to construct them) -- a systematic method for generating them, roughly a millennium before Pythagoras and a millennium and a half before Euclid's formula. M8 states this as historical context and must not present 'Pythagorean' as an authorship claim about the underlying arithmetic fact.
seeds.source_citation: Plimpton 322, Old Babylonian tablet, c. 1900-1600 BCE (G.A. Plimpton Collection, Columbia University) -- a table of Pythagorean-triple-related numbers predating Pythagoras by roughly a millennium. Wikipedia 'Plimpton 322'; ISAW/NYU exhibition 'Before Pythagoras: The Culture of Old Babylonian Mathematics' (isaw.nyu.edu/exhibitions/before-pythagoras).
